title: Periods and training: what's normal
summary: Know what's normal during a period, what often helps, when to see a doctor and who to talk to.

p: A period is a normal part of growing up, and tennis players at every level train and play with one. Most players do their sessions as usual.
In large studies of women who exercise, these symptoms were very common, and how strong they are changes from person to person:
list: Cramps and pain in the lower belly.
Tiredness.
Changes in mood and motivation.
Tender or sore breasts.
sections.callout: A period on its own isn't a reason to hide it or drop training. Tell an adult about any symptom that worries you.

p: Sessions are done as written. If pain stops you doing a move, follow the pain ladder in the lesson "Pain or soreness? And the red flags", which tells you what to do with that move.
No study has found core work harmful during a period.
If any of these happen mid-session, stop and tell an adult:
list: Dizziness or feeling close to fainting.
More breathless than usual for the same effort.
Pain that doubles you over.
sections.callout: The pain ladder is for a move that hurts. If you start a session feeling flat or unwell, talk to a parent and your coach.

p: In research reviews, heat and regular exercise reduced period pain. The evidence is low quality, and for exercise the result comes from weeks of regular training and not from a single session.
list: Heat: a hot water bottle or heat pack on the lower belly. In one review, heat worked about as well as painkillers, or better.
Regular training through the month, which is already part of this programme.
Walking and easy movement: some athletes feel it helps, though we have no direct research on a single day.
sections.warn: Painkillers, tablets or any supplement only with a parent's knowledge and a doctor's advice.
sections.callout: If none of this helps, show a doctor any pain that keeps you away from school, training or matches.

p: A period is normal, but a doctor should look at some patterns. The numbers below are rough guides, and the doctor decides.
list: No first period by about age 15, or about 3 years after breast development started.
Periods that stop for 3 months or more after being regular.
Cycles that are often shorter than about 21 days or longer than about 45 days.
Very heavy bleeding: soaking a pad or tampon every 1 to 2 hours, bleeding for longer than about 7 days, or new dizziness, breathlessness or tiredness.
Pain that doubles you over, makes you miss school or sport, or doesn't ease with heat and easy movement.
sections.warn: Very heavy bleeding with dizziness, breathlessness or new weakness: tell a parent or another adult the same day and get medical help. Emergency number: 115 in Iran.
sections.callout: Under 18: tell a parent or an adult you trust, and book a doctor.

p: Heavy bleeding is common in athletes. In surveys of women who exercise, 36% to 54% reported it, about a third had a past diagnosis of anaemia, and only 22% had sought medical advice.
If your bleeding is heavy or you're tired all the time, ask a doctor to check your iron. Don't start iron tablets on your own.
sections.callout: Iron tablets only after a blood test and a doctor's advice.

sections.h: A missed period isn't a fitness sign
p: Periods that stop or turn irregular aren't a sign of high fitness. They can show that your body isn't getting enough energy for the training you do, which is called low energy availability.

This can lead to missed periods, stress fractures and constant tiredness. Some researchers say the evidence shows links more than proof of cause, and that's why a doctor needs to see the whole picture.
sections.warn: If your periods stop or are irregular, tell a parent and see a doctor. Never praise a player for how her body looks.
sections.callout: A period that stops in an athlete is a sign for a doctor to look at.

p: Talk to a parent or an adult you trust. For some players a female coach is the easiest choice, and for others it's their mother.

Painkillers, iron tablets and hormonal contraception, including the pill, are for you, a parent and a doctor to decide, and a coach doesn't suggest them. If you track your cycle, the record is for your doctor and it isn't a performance tool.
list: A parent.
A female coach or another adult you trust.
A doctor or family doctor.
sections.callout: You don't have to say everything at once. Start with one sentence: "My period hurts and I'd like to talk about it."

sections.h: What coaches and parents should and shouldn't say
p: This part is for coaches and parents. A period is a private matter, so talk about it with respect and never in front of others.
list: Ask how she feels and listen.
Let her say what she needs.
If you're worried, talk with her and her parents about seeing a doctor.
Don't say "you're making excuses" or "you've gone soft because of your period".
Don't talk about her weight or how her body looks.
Don't suggest painkillers, tablets or supplements. That decision belongs to the family and a doctor.
sections.callout: Ask, listen, and leave medical decisions to the family and a doctor.
